title: Section 102 — Culpable homicide by causing death of person other than person whose death was intended

content.overview: BNS s. 102 — Culpable homicide by causing death of person other than person whose death was intended.
content.study:
Introduction and meaning
Culpable homicide by causing death of person other than person whose death was intended. BNS restatement of IPC 301. Elements are substantially the same; cite the BNS number for offences on or after 1 July 2024. BNS restatement of IPC 301. Cite the BNS number for facts on or after 1 July 2024.
In student language: BNS s. 102 is the rule on “Culpable homicide by causing death of person other than person whose death was intended”. The section provides that if a person, by doing anything which he intends or knows to be likely to cause death, commits culpable homicide by causing the death of any person, whose death he neither intends nor knows himself to be likely to cause, the culpable homicide committed by the offender is of the description of which it would have been if he had caused the death of the person whose death he intended or knew himself to be likely to cause. Do not stop at the heading. An examiner awards marks for the ingredients, the explanations and the illustrations, not for writing the title alone.

Why this is asked
Criminal law arguments turn on statutory ingredients. BNS s. 102 exists so that “Culpable homicide by causing death of person other than person whose death was intended” has a closed legal test in Chapter VI — Of Offences Affecting the Human Body. An authoritative analysis defines the concept, lists every ingredient, walks the statutory illustrations, states exceptions, and applies the test methodically to facts.
Chapter setting: Homicide, organised crime, terrorism, hurt, acid, restraint, assault, kidnapping and trafficking.

The provision in detail

learningObjectives: Master the doctrine of transferred malice (translatio criminis) codified under BNS s. 102.
Understand how criminal culpability transfers when an act aimed at one person kills another.
Differentiate between intended target, actual victim, and transferred mens rea.
Recognize that the description of homicide is identical to what it would have been had the intended person died.
enhancement.definition: BNS s. 102 codifies the doctrine of transferred malice, providing that if a person, by doing anything which he intends or knows to be likely to cause death, commits culpable homicide by causing the death of any person whose death he neither intends nor knows himself to be likely to cause, the culpable homicide committed is of the description of which it would have been if he had caused the death of the person whose death he intended or knew himself to be likely to cause.
enhancement.legalPrinciple: The doctrine of transferred malice holds that an offender's criminal intent to kill travels with the physical act; missing the intended target and killing an innocent bystander attracts identical homicidal culpability.
statutoryFramework: Chapter VI — Of Offences Affecting the Human Body, BNS s. 102 (corresponding to IPC s. 301).
Condition: Doing an act with intention or knowledge to cause death.
Transferred outcome: Causing the death of an unintended third person.
Legal consequence: The homicide is of the exact description (murder or culpable homicide not amounting to murder) as if the intended target had died.
Doctrinal maxim: Translatio criminis (transfer of criminal intent).
essentialIngredients: The accused did an act with the intention or knowledge of causing death to a person (Person A).
The act caused the death of another person (Person B).
The accused neither intended nor knew himself likely to cause the death of Person B.
The culpability for the death of Person B is measured exactly as if Person A had been killed.
enhancement.detailedExplanation: Section 102 embodies the well-established common law doctrine of transferred malice (translatio criminis). Where an offender shoots, stabs, or poisons with intent to kill target A, but due to bad aim, deflection, or intervention the blow strikes bystander B and kills B, the law does not permit the offender to argue: 'I had no mens rea against B.' The homicidal intention directed against A is transferred by operation of law to the fatal outcome suffered by B. The section specifies that the offence is of the exact description it would have been had A died: if killing A would have been murder under s. 101, killing B is murder; if killing A would have been covered by an Exception (e.g. grave and sudden provocation), killing B is culpable homicide not amounting to murder under s. 105.
examples: Teaching example (Bad aim killing bystander): An accused fires a pistol at his sworn enemy in a crowded alley with clear intent to assassinate him. The bullet misses the enemy, strikes an innocent pedestrian in the neck, and kills her. Under s. 102, the accused is guilty of murder of the pedestrian.

Teaching example (Poisoned meal eaten by another): An accused places lethal cyanide in a cup of coffee intended for his business partner. The partner passes the cup to a visiting guest who drinks it and dies. The malice is transferred to the guest; the accused is guilty of murder under s. 102.
distinctions: Section 102 vs Section 106 (Negligence): Section 102 requires a prior homicidal intention or knowledge directed at someone; Section 106 applies where there was no homicidal intention towards anyone, only rashness or negligence.

Transferred malice vs Mistake of identity: In transferred malice, the act misses target A and strikes B; in mistake of identity, the accused shoots B believing B is A (direct intent under factual mistake).
problemApplication: Issue: Whether an accused who planted a bomb under a political opponent's car, which detonated and killed the opponent's driver instead, can plead lack of intention towards the driver.
Rule: Under BNS s. 102, intent to cause death transfers to any person whose death is actually caused by the act.
Application: The accused intended to cause death by explosive detonation; the death of the driver was caused by that act.
Conclusion: The accused is guilty of murder of the driver by virtue of BNS s. 102.
